plain: Should students play on school teams that match their sex at birth rather than their gender identity? Proposition 134 on the November ballot would make that the rule at every school and college in Colorado.

short_version.text: Proposition 134 would set one statewide rule: school teams from elementary school through college divided by biological sex, plus open teams. Nobody tracks how many transgender athletes would be affected. The argument is fairness and safety for girls against inclusion, privacy and how sex would be checked.

agree_means: A yes vote on Proposition 134 requires every school team to be male, female or open to all, set by biological sex. Transgender students would play on open teams or on the team for their sex at birth.
disagree_means: A no vote leaves schools, districts and athletic associations to set their own rules under current state and federal law. Policies would keep varying by district.

example.text: Today a transgender girl at one high school may play on the girls' team after a school review, while a district next door bars her. Under Proposition 134, she could play only on an open team or the team for her sex at birth.

unknowns.text: How Proposition 134 would work with state anti-discrimination law is unsettled. A federal judge dismissed several districts' suit against the state in August 2026, and it is not clear what that means.

research_notes: All pages were fetched directly; none needed the browser. Claude in Chrome was not connected. Double-check: (1) The Blue Book source date (2026-09-11) is the PDF creation date; the PDF was modified Sept 24, 2026. (2) The number of transgender athletes in Colorado is not available: the Colorado Sun reports the high school association does not track it. The only count found, 61 male students on girls teams in Jeffco, is the U.S. Education Department's claim, which the Denver Post could not verify. (3) The Blue Book (drafted before Aug 31, 2026) says part of the districts' lawsuit challenging the state anti-discrimination law is ongoing; the Denver Post/Chalkbeat reported on Aug 31, 2026 that a federal judge dismissed the districts' suit against the state for lack of standing. The unknowns item reflects the later report. (4) The Supreme Court (West Virginia v. B.P.J. and Little v. Hecox, June 30, 2026) held states may limit girls' teams by biological sex; it did not require them to. (5) No peer-reviewed research on athletic advantage or on mental-health effects of sports exclusion was fetched, so those points appear only as attributed arguments (Blue Book, Colorado Sun, Supreme Court majority). (6) The Colorado Sun and Chalkbeat/Denver Post pieces quote advocates on both sides; Protect Kids Colorado supports and a coalition including One Colorado opposes. (7) Dollar figure: Jeffco is described as at risk of losing $50 million (Colorado Sun), not a confirmed loss.
